script.opening: "Hi — it’s just my back really, I’ve had it for the best part of a year. I lift heavy at work and I train a lot, so I’m sure I’ve just done it in. It’s annoying but I push through. I think I just need a referral for some physio or maybe a scan to check I haven’t slipped a disc. The weird thing is it’s actually worse when I rest and loosens up once I get moving — but that’s just stiffness, isn’t it?"

facts.text: If explored: this is INFLAMMATORY back pain, not mechanical — onset <40, insidious, >3 months, morning stiffness >30 min, night pain (waking in the second half of the night), improvement WITH exercise and worsening with rest, alternating buttock pain. This pattern suggests axial spondyloarthritis (e.g. ankylosing spondylitis), not a gym injury.

On direct questioning: a past painful RED EYE (possible anterior uveitis) — an extra-articular feature of spondyloarthritis. May also have a family history of "arthritis of the spine" or psoriasis/IBD if asked. He dismisses the eye as unrelated.

facts.topic: The cauda equina screen — MUST ASK
facts.text: CRITICAL safety screen (currently negative but must be asked): no saddle anaesthesia, no bladder/bowel dysfunction (retention/incontinence), no bilateral leg weakness/numbness, no progressive neurological deficit. These would be a SURGICAL EMERGENCY (cauda equina syndrome) needing emergency MRI/referral. Asking and documenting this is essential even when the story is inflammatory.

HIDDEN AGENDA — his "it’s just mechanical, I push through" masks anxiety he won’t voice: the night pain and fatigue are wearing him down, affecting his mood and his relationship, and he’s quietly frightened it’s "something serious / I’ll end up disabled" (an uncle has bad ankylosing spondylitis and is stooped). He’s also worried about his physically demanding job and being unable to work. He downplays to avoid bad news.

Officially: physio or a scan for a presumed disc/mechanical injury. What he needs: recognition of the inflammatory back-pain pattern → rheumatology referral for suspected axial SpA (NICE NG65), with inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 sent at referral if helpful (neither rules it out) and diagnostic imaging left to the rheumatology team (NICE NG65; NICE QS170), a documented cauda equina screen, and his fears about disability and work addressed.

ice.ideas: It’s a mechanical back injury from lifting and the gym; he needs physio or a scan for a disc.
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — the night pain and fatigue are grinding him down (mood, relationship), and he’s quietly frightened it’s "something serious / I’ll end up disabled" like an uncle with ankylosing spondylitis, and worried about his physical job; he downplays to avoid bad news.
ice.expectations: A physio referral or a scan for a disc. What he actually needs: recognition of inflammatory back pain, the right work-up and rheumatology referral for suspected axial SpA, a cauda equina screen, and his disability/work fears addressed.

cues: Back pain WORSE with rest / BETTER with exercise + night pain + morning stiffness >30min, onset <40 — inflammatory, not mechanical.
A past painful red eye — possible uveitis; an extra-articular spondyloarthritis clue he dismisses.
"I push through / just mechanical" — minimising; fear of disability (uncle with AS) and his physical job underneath.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the INFLAMMATORY back-pain pattern (age <40, insidious onset >3 months, morning stiffness >30 min, night pain, improvement WITH exercise and worse with rest, alternating buttock pain) and does NOT accept the "mechanical/gym injury" self-diagnosis; knows the NICE NG65 referral rule (back pain starting before 45 and lasting more than 3 months, with 4 or more of: onset before 35, waking in the second half of the night, buttock pain, improvement with movement, improvement within 48 hours of an NSAID, a first-degree relative with spondyloarthritis, current or past arthritis, enthesitis or psoriasis) — he has at least 4

Performs the CAUDA EQUINA / serious-pathology red-flag screen explicitly: saddle or perianal numbness, bladder/bowel dysfunction, sexual dysfunction, bilateral/progressive leg neurology (GIRFT national suspected cauda equina pathway, 2023) — and knows these would mandate EMERGENCY MRI/referral (and screens other red flags: weight loss, fever, history of cancer, etc.)

Elicits extra-articular/associated features of spondyloarthritis: uveitis (the past red eye), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis, dactylitis, family history (a first-degree relative counts towards NG65; his uncle is second-degree, so does not count, but matters to him), and good response to NSAIDs

Arranges the appropriate referral: refers to RHEUMATOLOGY for suspected axial spondyloarthritis (NICE NG65 — he meets 4 or more criteria); may send ESR/CRP and HLA-B27 with the referral but does not rule the diagnosis out on a normal result or let bloods delay it (NICE NG65); leaves diagnostic imaging (MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine) to the rheumatology team (NICE NG65; NICE QS170) — rather than ordering sacroiliac imaging itself or only physio/disc imaging

Manages symptoms and function meanwhile: NSAIDs first line (NICE NG65; dose per BNF; consider gastroprotection) and a specialist physiotherapy structured exercise programme (which genuinely helps inflammatory back pain), explaining the diagnosis is treatable
Hears the minimisation as fear and gently surfaces the disability worry (the uncle with AS) and the impact on mood/relationship/work, rather than accepting "I just push through"

Gives realistic, hopeful information: axial SpA is treatable (NSAIDs, exercise, biologics if needed) and early diagnosis improves outcomes — countering the "I’ll end up disabled" fear without false reassurance

Safety-nets clearly: cauda equina red flags (saddle numbness, bladder/bowel change, progressive leg weakness) → emergency same-day/A&E; arranges the rheumatology referral (bloods alongside; imaging decided by rheumatology); a recurrent painful red eye with light sensitivity or blurred vision → same-day eye assessment; addresses work and mood; documents the red-flag screen and follows up

worked.txt: "Can I pick up on the thing you called ‘weird’ — that it’s worse when you rest and eases when you move? That’s actually really important. A simple mechanical or disc problem is usually the opposite: worse with activity, better with rest. Pain that wakes you in the night and is stiff for ages in the morning but loosens with exercise points to an INFLAMMATORY kind of back problem, which is a different thing entirely — and one we can treat well."

"Before we go further, I need to check a few safety things, and I ask everyone these. Any numbness in the saddle area — where you’d sit on a bike? Any change in controlling your bladder or bowels, or going numb or weak in both legs? … Good, none of that. If any of those ever happen, that’s a 999 / A&E emergency the same day, because of the nerves at the base of the spine. Worth you knowing that."

"You mentioned a painful red eye a while back — I don’t think that’s unrelated. This kind of inflammatory back condition can come with eye inflammation, and sometimes psoriasis or gut problems, and it can run in families. Does anyone in the family have arthritis of the spine? … Your uncle. That fits the picture I’m thinking of."

"Can I gently ask — watching your uncle, stooped and struggling, has part of you been frightened that’s where this is heading, and that with your job you’d not be able to work? … That makes complete sense, and I’m really glad you said it. Here’s the important bit: catching this early, like now, is exactly what changes that outcome. The picture for people diagnosed today is very different from your uncle’s generation."

"So rather than just physio for a disc, I want to do this properly: refer you to the joint specialists — rheumatology — for what we call axial spondyloarthritis. I’ll send some blood tests and a specific gene test with the referral, though a normal result wouldn’t rule it out, and the specialists will decide on the right scans of your lower spine and pelvis. Meanwhile, regular anti-inflammatories and — counter-intuitively — keeping up exercise and physio genuinely help this, so don’t stop training, we’ll just guide it."

"To be straight: I can’t promise what the tests show, but inflammatory back pain is treatable — anti-inflammatories, exercise, and if needed there are very effective modern treatments that didn’t exist in your uncle’s day. Early action is on your side. And remember the emergency signs — saddle numbness, bladder or bowel changes, weak legs — that’s straight to A&E. If that red eye comes back, painful and light-sensitive, get it checked the same day. Otherwise, let’s get the tests and the referral moving, and I’ll see you to go through them. You came thinking gym injury; what we’re doing is catching something early enough to stay ahead of it."

f.learning: Chronic low back pain in a young adult that is WORSE with rest and BETTER with exercise, with night pain and prolonged morning stiffness, onset <40 and alternating buttock pain, is INFLAMMATORY back pain (suggesting axial spondyloarthritis), not a mechanical/gym injury — and must not be accepted as such. The action is rheumatology referral under NICE NG65 (he meets 4 or more criteria), with inflammatory markers and HLA-B27 sent alongside if helpful — neither rules it out — and diagnostic imaging (MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine) left to rheumatology (NICE NG65; NICE QS170), plus first-line NSAIDs and a structured exercise/physiotherapy programme (which genuinely help). Extra-articular clues — a past painful red eye (uveitis), psoriasis, IBD, family history — support the diagnosis. Crucially, even when the story is inflammatory, the CAUDA EQUINA red-flag screen must be performed and documented (saddle anaesthesia, bladder/bowel or sexual dysfunction, bilateral/progressive leg neurology → emergency MRI/A&E; GIRFT 2023). The hidden agenda is fear masked by "I just push through": dread of disability (an uncle with ankylosing spondylitis), impact on mood/relationship, and worry about a physically demanding job. Surface it, give realistic hope (early diagnosis transforms outcomes; effective treatments exist), and safety-net the cauda equina emergency clearly.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG65 (Spondyloarthritis in over 16s, 2017) · NICE QS170 (2018) · NICE NG59 (Low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated July 2026) · GIRFT national suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway (2023) · NICE TA383 (2016) · BNF
knowledge.summary: Nine months of back and buttock pain in a 28-year-old that is worse with rest, better with movement and wakes him in the second half of the night is inflammatory back pain. He meets NICE NG65 criteria for rheumatology referral for suspected axial spondyloarthritis — after a documented cauda equina screen.

points.t: Low back pain that started before 45 and has lasted more than 3 months: refer to rheumatology for a spondyloarthritis assessment if 4 or more of — onset before 35; waking in the second half of the night; buttock pain; improvement with movement; improvement within 48 hours of an NSAID; a first-degree relative with spondyloarthritis; current or past arthritis, enthesitis or psoriasis. With exactly 3, test HLA-B27 and refer if positive. Aaron has at least 4.

points.h: Tests do not rule it out
points.t: NICE NG65: do not rule out spondyloarthritis on a negative HLA-B27 or normal CRP/ESR alone. Bloods are useful at referral but must not delay it. Diagnostic imaging (MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine when X-ray is normal or unsuitable) sits with the rheumatology team (NICE NG65; NICE QS170).

Acute anterior uveitis (a painful red eye with light sensitivity), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis and dactylitis all point towards spondyloarthritis. A second-degree relative (his uncle) does not count towards the NG65 criteria but still matters to him.

GIRFT (2023): new bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle or perianal numbness, sexual dysfunction, or bilateral or progressive leg weakness or sensory change needs emergency same-day assessment and MRI. Ask and document even when the story is inflammatory. Also ask about weight loss, fever, cancer history and immunosuppression (NICE NG59).

NICE NG65: NSAIDs first line (dose per BNF; consider gastroprotection) and a specialist physiotherapy structured exercise programme. NICE TA383: TNF-alpha inhibitors for axial spondyloarthritis that remains active despite NSAIDs, under specialist care.
Anterior uveitis can recur. A painful red eye with light sensitivity or blurred vision needs same-day eye assessment, not conjunctivitis drops.

Physical warehouse job, gym, sleep, fatigue, mood and home life; uncle with ankylosing spondylitis.

Documented cauda equina screen (saddle anaesthesia, bladder, bowel, sexual function, bilateral leg symptoms) and systemic red flags.
Named inflammatory back pain and suspected axial spondyloarthritis in plain words, linked to the red eye.
After open exploration, used closed questions with clear signposting to confirm specific details.
Used information already available in the notes/referral; did not re-ask what was already documented or said.

Possible past anterior uveitis identified; mood and sleep acknowledged; work adjustments offered.

model.text: Hi Aaron, I’m Dr Lee. Can I just confirm your date of birth, and that you’re somewhere private? … Great. What’s been going on with your back?
model.why: Checks identity and privacy on video, then opens

model.text: It’s just my back really, best part of a year. I lift heavy at work and I train a lot, so I’ve probably done it in. I push through. I was thinking physio, or a scan to check I haven’t slipped a disc. Weird thing is it’s worse when I rest and loosens up once I get moving — that’s just stiffness though, isn’t it?
That last bit is actually really interesting, and I’d like to come back to it. Physio and a scan are both on the table. Can I ask some questions first, then we’ll decide together what’s best?
model.why: Flags the key cue and sets an agenda without promising a scan

model.text: Yeah, go for it.
Tell me about a typical day with it — mornings, nights, and how it is at work.
model.why: Open question about pattern and impact

model.text: Mornings I’m like an old man — takes me the best part of an hour to loosen up. It wakes me in the early hours and I have to get up and walk about. Once I’m moving at work it’s better.
Where exactly is the pain — just the lower back, or into the buttocks or legs?
model.why: Characterises the pain and looks for buttock pain and sciatica

model.text: Lower back, and my buttocks — sometimes one side, sometimes the other. Not down the legs.

I need to ask a few important safety questions I ask everyone with back pain. Any numbness around your bottom or between your legs, any change in how your bladder or bowels work, any problems with erections, or weakness or numbness in both legs?
model.why: Explicit cauda equina screen in plain language

model.text: No, none of that.
Good. Any weight loss, fevers or night sweats?
No. Just knackered from the sleep.
A few questions that might seem unrelated. Have you ever had a painful red eye, sore to light? Any skin rashes like psoriasis, bowel problems, or swollen joints or heels?
model.why: Looks for extra-articular features of spondyloarthritis

model.text: Actually — I had a really painful red eye a few months back. Couldn’t look at the light. It went on its own. Nothing else though. Is that connected?
It might be, and I’m glad you mentioned it. You’ve said a few times you push through. How is all this really affecting you?
model.why: Follows the minimising cue to the impact

model.text: (Pause.) Honestly, it’s grinding me down. Tired all the time, short with everyone at home. And my uncle’s got ankylosing spondylitis — he’s all bent over now. I’ve kind of been avoiding thinking it could be that.
Thank you for telling me — that’s a lot to carry quietly. So part of you has been worried this is what your uncle has, and what that might mean for you and your job?
model.why: Reflects the hidden fear back accurately

model.text: Yeah. My job’s all lifting. If I can’t do that, I don’t know what I’d do.

Let me be straight with you. Back pain that’s worse with rest, better with movement, wakes you in the second half of the night and moves between the buttocks, starting at your age — that’s what we call inflammatory back pain. With the red eye, it makes me think of a condition called axial spondyloarthritis, the family that ankylosing spondylitis belongs to. It isn’t a gym injury.
model.why: Names the inflammatory pattern and the working diagnosis

model.text: So it is what my uncle’s got.

It might be in the same family, and we need a specialist to confirm it. But your story isn’t his. Things have changed a lot — there are good treatments now, and catching it early, as we might be doing, gives you the best chance of staying active and working.
model.why: Gives realistic hope without false reassurance

model.text: Right. That’s… actually a relief, in a way. At least it’s got a name.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll refer you to the rheumatology team — they’re the right people, rather than a disc scan. They’ll organise the scan that looks at the joints at the base of your spine. I’d also like blood tests for inflammation and a gene marker called HLA-B27 to send with the referral — though normal results wouldn’t rule it out.
model.why: NICE NG65 referral with appropriate bloods; imaging via rheumatology

model.text: Okay. And the pain in the meantime?

Anti-inflammatories are the first treatment for this, taken regularly rather than now and then — I’ll prescribe one and talk about stomach protection. And your instinct to keep moving is right: I’ll refer you to physio for a proper exercise programme, which really helps this condition. Keep training — just nothing that makes things worse.
That’s good. I don’t want to stop the gym.

And for work — if lifting gets too much, I can do a fit note suggesting adjusted duties. You also mentioned being short with people at home. Would it help to talk more about how you’re feeling when I see you next?
model.why: Addresses work and mood as part of the plan

model.text: Yeah, maybe. I’d rather sort the back first.

Two important things. If you ever get numbness between your legs, problems passing water or controlling your bowels, or weakness in both legs, go to A&E straight away. And if the red eye comes back — painful, sore to light — get it seen the same day by an eye service, not the chemist.
model.why: Specific cauda equina and uveitis safety-nets

model.text: Numbness down below or bladder — A&E. Red eye — same day.
Exactly. Bloods this week, I’ll send the referral today, and let’s speak in two weeks to see how the tablets are working. Anything I’ve missed?
model.why: Dated follow-up and shares the floor

model.text: No — thanks, doc. Glad I finally mentioned the eye.

social.t: A warehouse job built on lifting. Fear of losing it drives his minimising; early adjustments and a clear plan protect his income.
Broken sleep and chronic pain are wearing him down and affecting home life. Offer to explore mood at follow-up; chronic inflammatory pain and low mood often travel together.

legal.t: A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with amended duties or altered hours, so he can keep working while treatment starts.

If confirmed, a long-term condition with a substantial effect on daily activities may meet the Act’s definition of disability, and his employer must then consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can help with costs.

professional.t: Axial spondyloarthritis is often diagnosed years late because young people’s back pain is assumed to be mechanical. Recognising the pattern is good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record the cauda equina screen, including negatives, and the safety-net given — especially in a remote consultation.

community.t: National Axial Spondyloarthritis Society (NASS) for information, exercise guidance and local groups; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if low mood persists.

playbook.diagnosis: Be clear about the pattern: “Back pain that’s worse with rest, better with movement, wakes you in the early hours and started before 35 is inflammatory back pain. With that red eye, I think this could be axial spondyloarthritis, and a rheumatologist needs to see you.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “A strained back is like a sprained ankle — it hurts more when you use it. Yours is the opposite: it stiffens when you rest, like a rusty hinge that frees up once it’s moving. That tells me it’s inflammation in the joints, not a strain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried this is what your uncle has, and about your job. Getting the right diagnosis early is exactly what gives you the best chance of staying at work and active.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him training and working with adjusted duties if needed; offer to explore mood and sleep at review; point him to NASS.
sharedPlan: Rheumatology referral (meets NICE NG65 criteria); CRP/ESR and HLA-B27 sent with it
Regular NSAID, consider gastroprotection; physiotherapy structured exercise programme
Fit note with amended duties if needed; review in 2 weeks
safetyNet: Numbness between the legs, bladder or bowel change, weakness in both legs — A&E
Painful red eye sore to light — same-day eye assessment

pitfalls.intro: This station hands you the diagnosis in the opening line. It is failed by candidates who hear “gym” and “disc” instead of “worse when I rest”, and by those who forget the safety screen once they have spotted the pattern.

items.fail: Agreeing to physio or a lumbar MRI for a presumed disc.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” He meets NICE NG65 criteria for rheumatology referral.
items.fix: Count the criteria aloud — onset before 35, night waking, buttock pain, better with movement — and refer.

items.fail: Skipping the cauda equina questions because the story sounds inflammatory.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Examiners expect the screen asked and documented in every back pain case.
items.fix: Ask saddle numbness, bladder, bowel, sexual function and both-leg symptoms in plain words.

items.fail: Never asking about eyes, skin or bowels.
items.why: The past red eye is the second clue; without it, the diagnosis rests on history alone.
items.fix: “Have you ever had a painful red eye, sore to the light?” Then link it for him.

items.fail: Telling him normal bloods would rule it out.
items.why: NICE NG65: a negative HLA-B27 or normal CRP/ESR does not exclude spondyloarthritis.
items.fix: Send bloods with the referral, but say clearly they don’t decide it.

items.fail: Accepting “I push through” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The uncle, the tiredness and the job are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “How is this really affecting you?” Then reflect the fear back before explaining.

items.fail: Safety-netting only “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name cauda equina symptoms with A&E, and a painful red eye with same-day eye care; book review.

Fatigue, mood, home life, the uncle with ankylosing spondylitis and a job built on lifting. Surface the fear behind “I push through”.
Inflammatory back pain and suspected axial spondyloarthritis. NICE NG65 rheumatology referral, bloods, regular NSAID, physiotherapy, work adjustments.
Cauda equina symptoms mean A&E. A recurrent red eye means same-day eye service. Review in 2 weeks. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Accepts “gym injury”, refers to physio or requests a lumbar MRI for a disc; never asks about rest versus activity or night pain; no cauda equina screen; the red eye never comes up; the uncle and the fear stay hidden.
wordPics.pass: Recognises the inflammatory pattern, screens cauda equina red flags, refers to rheumatology, starts NSAIDs and exercise, and gives a basic safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: counts the NICE NG65 criteria out loud; finds the past uveitis and links it; surfaces the uncle and the job worry and gives realistic hope; explains that normal bloods would not rule it out; adds a same-day red-eye safety-net and a work plan.

avoid.dont: “It sounds like you’ve strained it lifting — I’ll refer you to physio.”
avoid.instead: “Pain that’s worse with rest and better with movement makes me think of inflammation, not a strain.”
avoid.why: Accepting the mechanical label misses the diagnosis the station is built on.

avoid.dont: “Your bloods are normal, so it’s not ankylosing spondylitis.”
avoid.instead: “Normal blood tests don’t rule this out — the specialist will look at the whole picture.”
avoid.why: NICE NG65: do not exclude spondyloarthritis on normal CRP/ESR or a negative HLA-B27 alone.

avoid.dont: “Don’t worry, you won’t end up like your uncle.”
avoid.instead: “Your story isn’t his — treatment has changed a lot, and catching it early helps.”
avoid.why: Honest, specific hope scores; blanket reassurance does not.

SCA_MODELS.text: It’s just my back really, best part of a year. I lift heavy at work and I train a lot, so I’ve probably done it in. I push through. I was thinking physio, or a scan to check I haven’t slipped a disc. Weird thing is it’s worse when I rest and loosens up once I get moving — that’s just stiffness though, isn’t it?
That last bit is actually really interesting, and I’d like to come back to it. Physio and a scan are both on the table. Can I ask some questions first, then we’ll decide together what’s best?
SCA_MODELS.why: Flags the key cue and sets an agenda without promising a scan

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, go for it.
Tell me about a typical day with it — mornings, nights, and how it is at work.
SCA_MODELS.why: Open question about pattern and impact

SCA_MODELS.text: Mornings I’m like an old man — takes me the best part of an hour to loosen up. It wakes me in the early hours and I have to get up and walk about. Once I’m moving at work it’s better.
Where exactly is the pain — just the lower back, or into the buttocks or legs?
SCA_MODELS.why: Characterises the pain and looks for buttock pain and sciatica

SCA_MODELS.text: Lower back, and my buttocks — sometimes one side, sometimes the other. Not down the legs.

I need to ask a few important safety questions I ask everyone with back pain. Any numbness around your bottom or between your legs, any change in how your bladder or bowels work, any problems with erections, or weakness or numbness in both legs?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explicit cauda equina screen in plain language

SCA_MODELS.text: No, none of that.
Good. Any weight loss, fevers or night sweats?
No. Just knackered from the sleep.
A few questions that might seem unrelated. Have you ever had a painful red eye, sore to light? Any skin rashes like psoriasis, bowel problems, or swollen joints or heels?
SCA_MODELS.why: Looks for extra-articular features of spondyloarthritis

SCA_MODELS.text: Actually — I had a really painful red eye a few months back. Couldn’t look at the light. It went on its own. Nothing else though. Is that connected?
It might be, and I’m glad you mentioned it. You’ve said a few times you push through. How is all this really affecting you?
SCA_MODELS.why: Follows the minimising cue to the impact

SCA_MODELS.text: (Pause.) Honestly, it’s grinding me down. Tired all the time, short with everyone at home. And my uncle’s got ankylosing spondylitis — he’s all bent over now. I’ve kind of been avoiding thinking it could be that.
Thank you for telling me — that’s a lot to carry quietly. So part of you has been worried this is what your uncle has, and what that might mean for you and your job?
SCA_MODELS.why: Reflects the hidden fear back accurately

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah. My job’s all lifting. If I can’t do that, I don’t know what I’d do.

Let me be straight with you. Back pain that’s worse with rest, better with movement, wakes you in the second half of the night and moves between the buttocks, starting at your age — that’s what we call inflammatory back pain. With the red eye, it makes me think of a condition called axial spondyloarthritis, the family that ankylosing spondylitis belongs to. It isn’t a gym injury.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the inflammatory pattern and the working diagnosis

SCA_MODELS.text: So it is what my uncle’s got.

It might be in the same family, and we need a specialist to confirm it. But your story isn’t his. Things have changed a lot — there are good treatments now, and catching it early, as we might be doing, gives you the best chance of staying active and working.
SCA_MODELS.why: Gives realistic hope without false reassurance

SCA_MODELS.text: Right. That’s… actually a relief, in a way. At least it’s got a name.

Here’s what I suggest. I’ll refer you to the rheumatology team — they’re the right people, rather than a disc scan. They’ll organise the scan that looks at the joints at the base of your spine. I’d also like blood tests for inflammation and a gene marker called HLA-B27 to send with the referral — though normal results wouldn’t rule it out.
SCA_MODELS.why: NICE NG65 referral with appropriate bloods; imaging via rheumatology

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. And the pain in the meantime?

Anti-inflammatories are the first treatment for this, taken regularly rather than now and then — I’ll prescribe one and talk about stomach protection. And your instinct to keep moving is right: I’ll refer you to physio for a proper exercise programme, which really helps this condition. Keep training — just nothing that makes things worse.
That’s good. I don’t want to stop the gym.

And for work — if lifting gets too much, I can do a fit note suggesting adjusted duties. You also mentioned being short with people at home. Would it help to talk more about how you’re feeling when I see you next?
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses work and mood as part of the plan

SCA_MODELS.text: Yeah, maybe. I’d rather sort the back first.

Two important things. If you ever get numbness between your legs, problems passing water or controlling your bowels, or weakness in both legs, go to A&E straight away. And if the red eye comes back — painful, sore to light — get it seen the same day by an eye service, not the chemist.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific cauda equina and uveitis safety-nets

SCA_MODELS.text: Numbness down below or bladder — A&E. Red eye — same day.
Exactly. Bloods this week, I’ll send the referral today, and let’s speak in two weeks to see how the tablets are working. Anything I’ve missed?
SCA_MODELS.why: Dated follow-up and shares the floor

SCA_MODELS.text: No — thanks, doc. Glad I finally mentioned the eye.

SCA_STEM.name: Aaron Kelly
SCA_STEM.recent: No previous consultations for back pain on record. No bloods or imaging on file. Occupation: warehouse worker.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment: “back pain for most of a year — wants physio or a scan”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG65 (Spondyloarthritis in over 16s, 2017) · NICE QS170 (2018) · NICE NG59 (Low back pain and sciatica, 2016, updated July 2026) · GIRFT national suspected cauda equina syndrome pathway (2023) · NICE TA383 (2016) · BNF
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Nine months of back and buttock pain in a 28-year-old that is worse with rest, better with movement and wakes him in the second half of the night is inflammatory back pain. He meets NICE NG65 criteria for rheumatology referral for suspected axial spondyloarthritis — after a documented cauda equina screen.

points.t: Low back pain that started before 45 and has lasted more than 3 months: refer to rheumatology for a spondyloarthritis assessment if 4 or more of — onset before 35; waking in the second half of the night; buttock pain; improvement with movement; improvement within 48 hours of an NSAID; a first-degree relative with spondyloarthritis; current or past arthritis, enthesitis or psoriasis. With exactly 3, test HLA-B27 and refer if positive. Aaron has at least 4.

points.h: Tests do not rule it out
points.t: NICE NG65: do not rule out spondyloarthritis on a negative HLA-B27 or normal CRP/ESR alone. Bloods are useful at referral but must not delay it. Diagnostic imaging (MRI of the sacroiliac joints and spine when X-ray is normal or unsuitable) sits with the rheumatology team (NICE NG65; NICE QS170).

Acute anterior uveitis (a painful red eye with light sensitivity), psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, enthesitis and dactylitis all point towards spondyloarthritis. A second-degree relative (his uncle) does not count towards the NG65 criteria but still matters to him.

GIRFT (2023): new bladder or bowel dysfunction, saddle or perianal numbness, sexual dysfunction, or bilateral or progressive leg weakness or sensory change needs emergency same-day assessment and MRI. Ask and document even when the story is inflammatory. Also ask about weight loss, fever, cancer history and immunosuppression (NICE NG59).

NICE NG65: NSAIDs first line (dose per BNF; consider gastroprotection) and a specialist physiotherapy structured exercise programme. NICE TA383: TNF-alpha inhibitors for axial spondyloarthritis that remains active despite NSAIDs, under specialist care.
Anterior uveitis can recur. A painful red eye with light sensitivity or blurred vision needs same-day eye assessment, not conjunctivitis drops.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question; took his “worse when I rest” comment seriously instead of moving straight to physio or a scan.
Physical warehouse job, gym, sleep, fatigue, mood and home life; uncle with ankylosing spondylitis.
Picked up “loosens up once I get moving” and “I push through”, and returned to both.
Idea (gym or disc injury); concern (ending up like his uncle, losing his job); expectation (physio or a scan).
Recognised video limits; planned CRP/ESR and HLA-B27 without delaying referral; knew diagnostic imaging is rheumatology-led.
Inflammatory versus mechanical back pain; disc and sciatica; serious pathology (infection, malignancy).
Documented cauda equina screen (saddle anaesthesia, bladder, bowel, sexual function, bilateral leg symptoms) and systemic red flags.
Named inflammatory back pain and suspected axial spondyloarthritis in plain words, linked to the red eye.
Rheumatology referral meeting NICE NG65 criteria; regular NSAID with gastroprotection considered; physiotherapy structured exercise.
Possible past anterior uveitis identified; mood and sleep acknowledged; work adjustments offered.
Cauda equina and red-eye safety-nets in plain words; referral sent today, review in 2 weeks.

social.t: A warehouse job built on lifting. Fear of losing it drives his minimising; early adjustments and a clear plan protect his income.
Broken sleep and chronic pain are wearing him down and affecting home life. Offer to explore mood at follow-up; chronic inflammatory pain and low mood often travel together.

legal.t: A fit note can advise “may be fit for work” with amended duties or altered hours, so he can keep working while treatment starts.

If confirmed, a long-term condition with a substantial effect on daily activities may meet the Act’s definition of disability, and his employer must then consider reasonable adjustments. Access to Work can help with costs.

professional.t: Axial spondyloarthritis is often diagnosed years late because young people’s back pain is assumed to be mechanical. Recognising the pattern is good clinical care (GMC Good Medical Practice 2024).
Record the cauda equina screen, including negatives, and the safety-net given — especially in a remote consultation.

community.t: National Axial Spondyloarthritis Society (NASS) for information, exercise guidance and local groups; NHS Talking Therapies self-referral if low mood persists.

redFlags: Saddle anaesthesia, bladder or bowel change, sexual dysfunction, bilateral or progressive leg symptoms — emergency same-day assessment
Weight loss, fever, night sweats, cancer history, immunosuppression or IV drug use
Painful red eye with light sensitivity — possible anterior uveitis
psychosocial: Warehouse job built on lifting — fear of losing it
Poor sleep, fatigue, irritability at home
Uncle with ankylosing spondylitis, now stooped
ice: Idea: “I’ve done my back in lifting and at the gym.”
Concern: ending up like his uncle; not being able to work
Expectation: physio or a scan for a slipped disc

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Be clear about the pattern: “Back pain that’s worse with rest, better with movement, wakes you in the early hours and started before 35 is inflammatory back pain. With that red eye, I think this could be axial spondyloarthritis, and a rheumatologist needs to see you.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “A strained back is like a sprained ankle — it hurts more when you use it. Yours is the opposite: it stiffens when you rest, like a rusty hinge that frees up once it’s moving. That tells me it’s inflammation in the joints, not a strain.”

management.reflectIce: “You’ve been worried this is what your uncle has, and about your job. Getting the right diagnosis early is exactly what gives you the best chance of staying at work and active.”
management.psychosocial: Keep him training and working with adjusted duties if needed; offer to explore mood and sleep at review; point him to NASS.
sharedPlan: Rheumatology referral (meets NICE NG65 criteria); CRP/ESR and HLA-B27 sent with it
Regular NSAID, consider gastroprotection; physiotherapy structured exercise programme
Fit note with amended duties if needed; review in 2 weeks
safetyNet: Numbness between the legs, bladder or bowel change, weakness in both legs — A&E
Painful red eye sore to light — same-day eye assessment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station hands you the diagnosis in the opening line. It is failed by candidates who hear “gym” and “disc” instead of “worse when I rest”, and by those who forget the safety screen once they have spotted the pattern.

items.fail: Agreeing to physio or a lumbar MRI for a presumed disc.
items.why: “Management plan not in line with current UK best practice.” He meets NICE NG65 criteria for rheumatology referral.
items.fix: Count the criteria aloud — onset before 35, night waking, buttock pain, better with movement — and refer.

items.fail: Skipping the cauda equina questions because the story sounds inflammatory.
items.why: “Does not rule out serious disease.” Examiners expect the screen asked and documented in every back pain case.
items.fix: Ask saddle numbness, bladder, bowel, sexual function and both-leg symptoms in plain words.

items.fail: Never asking about eyes, skin or bowels.
items.why: The past red eye is the second clue; without it, the diagnosis rests on history alone.
items.fix: “Have you ever had a painful red eye, sore to the light?” Then link it for him.

items.fail: Telling him normal bloods would rule it out.
items.why: NICE NG65: a negative HLA-B27 or normal CRP/ESR does not exclude spondyloarthritis.
items.fix: Send bloods with the referral, but say clearly they don’t decide it.

items.fail: Accepting “I push through” and moving on.
items.why: “Does not identify or respond to cues.” The uncle, the tiredness and the job are the hidden agenda.
items.fix: “How is this really affecting you?” Then reflect the fear back before explaining.

items.fail: Safety-netting only “come back if it gets worse”.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name cauda equina symptoms with A&E, and a painful red eye with same-day eye care; book review.
